content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a generic plug-in model for passage re-ranking in information retrieval tasks. The key aspects of the model are the "hybrid" aspect combining both sparse lexical and dense semantic representations, and the "collaborative" aspect which boosts the ranking of passages based on their similarity to other high-ranking passages. Improved performance is shown on two benchmark datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The underlying intuitions seem sound and well-connected to the proposed model. For the most part it is well-written, clearly
organized, sufficiently detailed, and well-contextualized with respect to related work. The evaluation shows that the re-ranker delivers consistent improvements, and the ablation experiments generally support the claims about why the model works well.

I found the major weakness of the paper to be the lack of evaluation against other re-ranking approaches. The paper also repeatedly
references the computational efficiency of the approach, but doesn't fully commit to an explicit exploration or evaluation of that benefit.

The key "collaborative" assumption is that anchor passages resembling the other anchor passages are more likely to be relevant, and this assumption seems supported in the evaluation. This seems to possibly be missing some real-world utility of diversity or broader coverage in the returned results for general information retrieval. I guess this notion is not really represented in the benchmark datasets being used here which are focused on something more like Question Answering. Do the authors think this technique is truly general to all of information retrieval including cases where diversity or coverage matter, or is it best suited to more factual retrieval use cases?

Analysis - Ablation: "All experiments are performed on Natural Questions dataset with DPR-Multi retriever." - why this setting?

Analysis - Collaborative Feature: minor wording suggestions "by replace" -> "by replacing" and ", for not changing" -> "in order to
avoid changing". However, it seems like using random similarity information would potentially have a worse impact on performance than
omitting it from the re-ranking altogether (even if it requires altering the architecture). If so, this would artificially inflate the
benefit of the collaborative features. Is this concern accurate, and if so, is there some way to mitigate it?

Figure 2: what happens as L increases beyond 100? Presumably the quality eventually degrades as non-relevant passages get included into the anchor set and pollute the collaborative aspect? If so it would be interesting to see or at least mention it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity and level of detail are good, aside from the cost/performance/practical aspects. The novelty of non-linear collaborative interactions between sparse and dense features seems
justified.

Receptive Field and Complexity: this section was not very clear to me. Perhaps a diagram would have helped. It didn't seem essential to
the contribution of the paper, unless it is central to the computational cost argument which I mention below.

Is the lesser computation cost (versus what exactly?) one of the major contributions here? If so, it should be argued for more clearly in one
dedicated section instead of mentioned in passing across many sections of the paper.

Table 2: ANCE + HybRank R@50 difference in parentheses is missing + sign.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The approach seems promising, but the paper could be significantly improved by the inclusion of at least one re-ranking baseline. The
paper mentions efficiency, performance, and practical implementation advantages in a somewhat scattershot fashion across multiple sections of the paper - if this aspect is intended to be a core contribution, the presentation and evidence for it should be concentrated in a more tightly focused and structured way.

content.title: Response to Reviewer aG4A  (part 1)
content.comment:
Thanks for your positive comments on our approach and contructive suggestions on the writing and experiments. We will present the revision details and answer your questions below.

**I found the major weakness of the paper to be the lack of evaluation against other re-ranking approaches.** \
**The approach seems promising, but the paper could be significantly improved by the inclusion of at least one re-ranking baseline.**

In view of the limited time available, we have conducted supplementary experiments on two strong reranking methods, RocketQA and RocketQAv2. These two methods involve adversarial or joint training of retriever and rerankers, and thus provide powerful retriever as well as stronger reranker. The results shows that HybRank built upon their retrievers outperforms their rerankers on Natural Questions. Additionally, due to the plug-in property, HybRank can be built opon their rerankers, which further improves the performance on both datasets.

The following are results of supplementary experiments. More details can be found in the revised paper.

#### Supplementary Experiments on Natural Questions
| Methods                        |  R@1  |  R@5  |  R@20  |
| :----------------------------- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| RocketQA-retriever + HybRank   | 51.75 $\rightarrow$ 56.07 (**+4.32**) | 74.02 $\rightarrow$ 77.04 (**+3.02**) | 83.99 $\rightarrow$ 85.68 (**+1.69**) |
| RocketQA-reranker + HybRank    | 54.60 $\rightarrow$ 59.83 (**+5.23**) | 76.59 $\rightarrow$ 78.73 (**+2.14**) | 85.01 $\rightarrow$ 86.40 (**+1.39**) |
| RocketQAv2-retriever + HybRank | 55.57 $\rightarrow$ 56.98 (**+1.41**) | 75.98 $\rightarrow$ 76.65 (**+0.67**) | 84.46 $\rightarrow$ 85.76 (**+1.30**) |
| RocketQAv2-reranker + HybRank  | 57.17 $\rightarrow$ 59.50 (**+2.33**) | 75.98 $\rightarrow$ 78.34 (**+2.36**) | 84.71 $\rightarrow$ 86.26 (**+1.55**) |

#### Supplementary Experiments on MS MARCO
| Methods                        |  MRR@10  |  R@10  |  R@50  |
| :----------------------------- | :------: | :---: | :---: |
| RocketQA-retriever + HybRank   | 35.76 $\rightarrow$ 37.96 (**+2.20**) | 64.01 $\rightarrow$ 67.12 (**+3.11**) | 83.41 $\rightarrow$ 85.59 (**+2.18**) |
| RocketQA-reranker + HybRank    | 40.50 $\rightarrow$ 40.98 (**+0.48**) | 69.81 $\rightarrow$ 70.40 (**+0.59**) | 86.46 $\rightarrow$ 86.55 (**+0.09**) |
| RocketQAv2-retriever + HybRank  | 37.28 $\rightarrow$ 38.69 (**+1.41**) | 65.72 $\rightarrow$ 67.92 (**+2.20**) | 84.04 $\rightarrow$ 85.70 (**+1.66**) |
| RocketQAv2-reranker + HybRank  | 41.15 $\rightarrow$ 41.40 (**+0.25**) | 69.99 $\rightarrow$ 70.37 (**+0.38**) | 86.55 $\rightarrow$ 86.68 (**+0.13**) |

**The paper also repeatedly references the computational efficiency of the approach, but doesn't fully commit to an explicit exploration or evaluation of that benefit.**

We compare our model with BERT in typical reranking methods in terms of parameters, and draw the conclusion that our model is more lightweight.

|      | BERT-base | BERT-large | Our model |
| :--- | :-------: | :---------:| :-------: |
| layers | 12 | 24 | 2 + 1 |
| hidden size | 768 | 1024 | 64 |
| heads | 12 | 16 | 8 |
| total parameters | 110M | 340M | 0.22M |

Nevertheless, less computational cost is not the major contribution of our method. We have diminished the description of efficiency and put more emphasis on the hybrid and collaborative aspects in the revised paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer aG4A (part 2)
content.comment:
**Figure 2: what happens as L increases beyond 100? Presumably the quality eventually degrades as non-relevant passages get included into the anchor set and pollute the collaborative aspect? If so it would be interesting to see or at least mention it.**

The average relevance of anchors would degrade to a low lever, as you mentioned. Due to the O(L2) computational complexity of sequence aggregation in HybRank, it is hard to directly perform experiments on large L. 

Nevertheless, we design a simulation experiment for your questions. We randomly select L passages from the corpus as anchors for simulating the non-relevance anchor set. Experimental results below shows that random anchors slightly improves the performance but still lags far behind the relevant anchors, demonstrating the benefits of collaborative information and the predominance of the anchor quality.

| Methods    |  R@1  |  R@5  | R@10  | R@20  | R@50  |
| :--------- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| retriever  | 45.82 | 68.12 | 75.24 | 80.30 | 84.57 |
| r/d anchor | 46.18 | 68.84 | 75.43 | 80.91 | 85.01 |
| HybRank    | 51.99 | 72.71 | 79.03 | 83.24 | 85.93 |

More detailed analysis is in Section 4.4 Analysis of the revised paper.

**The key "collaborative" assumption is that anchor passages resembling the other anchor passages are more likely to be relevant, and this assumption seems supported in the evaluation. This seems to possibly be missing some real-world utility of diversity or broader coverage in the returned results for general information retrieval. I guess this notion is not really represented in the benchmark datasets being used here which are focused on something more like Question Answering. Do the authors think this technique is truly general to all of information retrieval including cases where diversity or coverage matter, or is it best suited to more factual retrieval use cases?**

Yes, two datasets in our evaluation focus on open-domain question answering. Diversity or broader coverage are not involved here. This is also the reason why we focus on "passage reranking", which is often used in open-domain question answering, rather than more general "information retrieval".

Although there is not enough time to conduct experiments on general information retrieval or factual retrieval cases, we validate the impact of collaborative information in extreme case described in previous question, where anchors are randomly selected. These experiments shows the potential of collaborative modeling. And we believe that with more elaborated anchor selection strategies, the collaborative assumption would generalize to more general cases. We are very interested in further exploring the collaborative modeling in our future work.

**Analysis - Ablation: "All experiments are performed on Natural Questions dataset with DPR-Multi retriever." - why this setting?**

We select the dataset and baseline retriever in consideration of time and clarity. On the one hand, experiments on Natural Question takes about 13 hours, while on MS MARCO takes about 4 days. On the other hand, HybRank brings the largest improvement on DPR-Multi retriever. Ablation study on this baseline would maximize the gaps between variants of HybRank, and reveal the effect of each components more clearly.

**However, it seems like using random similarity information would potentially have a worse impact on performance than omitting it from the re-ranking altogether (even if it requires altering the architecture). If so, this would artificially inflate the benefit of the collaborative features. Is this concern accurate, and if so, is there some way to mitigate it?**

Thanks for pointing it out. We think it is a legitimate concern. After careful consideration, we propose a slightly modified architecture to verify the benefit of collaborative features by omitting them altogether rather than replaced with random features. We observe similar results as before and the conclusions from ablation study of collaborative are not changed. We have substituted the modified architecture and new results for the original ones in the revised paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission studies passage reranking in the text domain. The intuition of this paper is to leverage interactions among top retrieved passages to enhance the ranking process. First, similarity matrices between query/passages and anchor passages (top L results) are built based on the retrievers. The similarities are fed into BERT for richer representation and CLS is used as final representation. Finally each query-doc pair is scored using the dot product between the vectors. Experiments are done on MSMARCO and NQ datasets which shows that reranker can improve upon retrieval results.

content.title: Response to Reviewer r4pr (part 1)
content.comment:
Thanks for your kind advice. We have carefully read your review and revised the paper, and will answer your questions point by point.

**From the title, introduction, etc., it seems the goal is passage reranking. However, The experiments do not compare with any other rerankers.**

In view of the limited time available, we have conducted supplementary experiments on two strong reranking methods, RocketQA and RocketQAv2. These two methods involve adversarial or joint training of retriever and rerankers, and thus provide powerful retriever as well as stronger reranker. The results shows that HybRank built upon their retrievers outperforms their rerankers on Natural Questions. Additionally, due to the plug-in property, HybRank can be built opon their rerankers, which further improves the performance on both datasets.

The following are results of supplementary experiments. More details can be found in the revised paper.

#### Supplementary Experiments on Natural Questions
| Methods                        |  R@1  |  R@5  |  R@20  |
| :----------------------------- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| RocketQA-retriever + HybRank   | 51.75 $\rightarrow$ 56.07 (**+4.32**) | 74.02 $\rightarrow$ 77.04 (**+3.02**) | 83.99 $\rightarrow$ 85.68 (**+1.69**) |
| RocketQA-reranker + HybRank    | 54.60 $\rightarrow$ 59.83 (**+5.23**) | 76.59 $\rightarrow$ 78.73 (**+2.14**) | 85.01 $\rightarrow$ 86.40 (**+1.39**) |
| RocketQAv2-retriever + HybRank | 55.57 $\rightarrow$ 56.98 (**+1.41**) | 75.98 $\rightarrow$ 76.65 (**+0.67**) | 84.46 $\rightarrow$ 85.76 (**+1.30**) |
| RocketQAv2-reranker + HybRank  | 57.17 $\rightarrow$ 59.50 (**+2.33**) | 75.98 $\rightarrow$ 78.34 (**+2.36**) | 84.71 $\rightarrow$ 86.26 (**+1.55**) |

#### Supplementary Experiments on MS MARCO
| Methods                        |  MRR@10  |  R@10  |  R@50  |
| :----------------------------- | :------: | :---: | :---: |
| RocketQA-retriever + HybRank   | 35.76 $\rightarrow$ 37.96 (**+2.20**) | 64.01 $\rightarrow$ 67.12 (**+3.11**) | 83.41 $\rightarrow$ 85.59 (**+2.18**) |
| RocketQA-reranker + HybRank    | 40.50 $\rightarrow$ 40.98 (**+0.48**) | 69.81 $\rightarrow$ 70.40 (**+0.59**) | 86.46 $\rightarrow$ 86.55 (**+0.09**) |
| RocketQAv2-retriever + HybRank  | 37.28 $\rightarrow$ 38.69 (**+1.41**) | 65.72 $\rightarrow$ 67.92 (**+2.20**) | 84.04 $\rightarrow$ 85.70 (**+1.66**) |
| RocketQAv2-reranker + HybRank  | 41.15 $\rightarrow$ 41.40 (**+0.25**) | 69.99 $\rightarrow$ 70.37 (**+0.38**) | 86.55 $\rightarrow$ 86.68 (**+0.13**) |

**If the goal is reranking, the model looks strange and the model power looks very weak. If the reviewer understands correctly, the entire model only uses similarities from retriever systems as inputs. There are no place that directly model, say, query-document interactions directly with raw inputs.**

We do not think using only similarities as inputs is a weakness. On the contrary, these similarities provide additional information from various retrievers, including word overlap and semantic relevance. incorporating interaction between raw inputs into our method may improve the performance, but requires more computations. Later, we will show the comparison between our model and raw inputs interaction based model.

**There is a rich literature on reranking models, where many leverage listwise context. See references in (Neural Re-ranking in Multi-stage Recommender Systems: A Review). The paper does not discuss any of them. Also, the intuition is similar to pseudo relevance feedback based approaches, which is not discussed.**

We have added discussions about related topic, including listwise context in Multi-stage Recommender systems and pseudo-relevance feedback, in Section 1 Introduction and 5 Related Work of the revised version.

For example, PRM [1] model the item list as a sequence and using Transformer to rerank the whole list. Our HybRank model the list in a different perspective, i.e., regards query and each passage in the list as a collaborative sequence, and measures the relevance according to these sequences. Several pseudo-relevance feedback approaches [2, 3, 4] aim to refine the query model with the top-retrieved documents, while our HybRank uses the collaborative information as representations not only for the query but also for the documents. Otherwise, explicitly modeling collaborative information in a sequence perspective is rarely exploit in pseudo-relevance feedback approaches.

**So the paper looks like a lightweight retriever aggregation method instead of full reranking. If that is the goal, the paper needs significant rewrite.**

We offer a reranking model able to be applied on arbitrary passage list, in spite of implemented by retriever aggregation. Extensive experiments have demonstrated the consistent improvement over various retrievers and even over other strong rerankers. We have rewritten the inappropriate expressions and made our contributions and goals more clear in the revised paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer r4pr (part 2)
content.comment:
**Also, most similarities need to be computed for this model in extra, and BERT model is involved, so it's arguably not lightweight.**

Actually, the computation cost of these similarities are much less than these cross-encoder based approaches. For example, with the pre-computed dense representations provided by dense retrievers, only a dot product of two vectors is required for dense similarity. In some special task, e.g., open-domain question answering, retrieval may be performed on a specific document collection and thus these similarities can be pre-computed for further acceleration.

We adopt the Transformer encoder in the Interaction and Aggregation of HybRank, and refer to it as BERT in the original paper. Our Transformer encoder share the same architecture with the original BERT [5], which is a pretrained Transformer encoder, but differs a lot in hyperparameters. Our model use less layers, less heads and smaller hidden size. The comparison between our model and original BERT [5] are presented in the table:

|      | BERT-base [5] | BERT-large [5] | Our model |
| :--- | :-------: | :---------:| :-------: |
| layers | 12 | 24 | 2 + 1 |
| hidden size | 768 | 1024 | 64 |
| heads | 12 | 16 | 8 |
| total parameters | 110M | 340M | 0.22M |

Thus, we draw the conclusion that our model is lightweight. Nevertheless, less computational cost is not the major contribution of our method. We have diminished the description of efficiency and put more emphasis on the hybrid and collaborative aspects in the revised paper. Besides, we rename the $\mathrm{BERT}^{inter}$ and $\mathrm{BERT}^{aggr}$ to $\mathrm{Trans}^{inter}$ and $\mathrm{Trans}^{aggr}$ to avoid ambiguity.

---

[1] Changhua Pei, Yi Zhang, Yongfeng Zhang, Fei Sun, Xiao Lin, Hanxiao Sun, Jian Wu, Peng Jiang, Junfeng Ge, Wenwu Ou, and Dan Pei. Personalized Re-Ranking for Recommendation. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Recommender Systems, pp. 3-11. Association for Computing Machinery, 2019.

[2] Ben He and Iadh Ounis. Finding Good Feedback Documents. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, pp. 2011–2014. Association for Computing Machinery, 2009.

[3] Hamed Zamani and W Bruce Croft. Estimating Embedding Vectors for Queries. In Proceedings of the ACM International Conference on the Theory of Information Retrieval, pp. 123-132, 2016.

[4] Hamed Zamani, Javid Dadashkarimi, Azadeh Shakery, andW. Bruce Croft. Pseudo-Relevance Feedback Based on Matrix Factorization. In Proceedings of the 25th ACM International on Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, pp. 1483-1492. ACM, 2016.

[5] Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding. In Proceedings of the Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, pp. 4171-4186. Association for Computational Linguistics, 2019.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2aeu
content.comment:
Thanks for your kind advice. We apologize for missing discussions on related works. 

We have conducted a more sufficient survey on these works, and removed the improper claims about "ignore the relationship between passages".

Additionally, we have added discussions about these related approaches in Section 1 Introduction and 5 Related Work of the revised paper, including the learning to rank and pseudo-relevance feedback (PRF) works as you mentioned. 

**[1] Rahimi, Razieh, et al. "Building a multi-domain comparable corpus using a learning to rank method." Natural Language Engineering 22.4 (2016): 627-653**

Rahimi, et al. [1] adopt pairwise learning to rank algorithm to rank candidate target documents for each source document. They use different relevance metrics between source document and target documents as input features, and consider ordinal relationship between documents in the training data construction of Ranking SVM model. 

Differently, our HybRank takes the relevance metrics not only between the source (query) and targets (passages), but also between targets and targets, which form the proposed collaborative sequences. Moreover, we directly use these collaborative information as input features rather than for training data construction. The ordinal relationship is also encoded into input features in the form of positional encoding.

**[2] Zamani, Hamed, et al. "Pseudo-relevance feedback based on matrix factorization." Proceedings of the 25th ACM international on conference on information and knowledge management. 2016.**

Zamani, et al. [2] formulate the PRF task as a collaborative recommendation problem. Non-negative matrix factorization is utilized to cope with the sparsity characteristic of PRF task, i.e., to predict the weight of terms that have not appeared in the query. Both their work and our HybRank are inspired by collaborative recommendation system and explore the information of pseudo-relevant documents.

Although both their work and our HybRank combine query and top-retrieved documents, the modeling perspectives are totally different. We explicitly extract the collaborative information for the representations of not only the query, but also the documents, while Zamani, et al. [2] focus on enhancing the term weight estimation of query with top-retrived documents. Besides, we leverage the collaborative information to mix the lexical and semantic aspects of different retrievers, which is not achieved in [2].

content.title: Response to Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their valuable and insightful feedbacks. We are glad that they found the underlying intuitions in our approach seem sound and well-connected to the proposed model ($\color{purple} aG4A$). We are delighted to see that they found the experiments generally support the claim about the model ($\color{purple} aG4A$). We are also encouraged by their approvals on the clarity and well-organized writing ($\color{blue} 2aeu$, $\color{green} r4pr$, $\color{purple} aG4A$), detailed explanations ($\color{blue} 2aeu$, $\color{purple} aG4A$) and well-contextualized with respect to related work ($\color{purple} aG4A$).

We found the feedbacks very helpful for our work and update the manuscript according to their suggestions. Main points of the revision are summarized briefly below.

* We have supplemented missing comparisons and discussions, including reranker baselines ($\color{blue} 2aeu$, $\color{green} r4pr$, $\color{purple} aG4A$), discussions about learning to rank ($\color{blue} 2aeu$), pseudo-relevance feedback ($\color{blue} 2aeu$, $\color{green} r4pr$) and multi-stage recommendation ($\color{green} r4pr$).

* We have modified improper claims about the existing work ($\color{blue} 2aeu$, $\color{green} r4pr$) and computational efficiency ($\color{green} r4pr$, $\color{purple} aG4A$).

* We put more emphasis on our major contributions in the revised paper. Contents about the receptive field ($\color{purple} aG4A$) have been moved to the appendix. Scattershot statements on computational efficiency have been removed.

* Insightful questions about the generalization and anchors ($\color{purple} aG4A$) are discussed in the individual response or validated in supplementary experiments.

We have addressed the concerns of the reviewers in individual responses and are happy to participate in any further discussions.
